history.heading: Indigenous peoples
paragraphs: Indigenous peoples have lived in what is now Canada for thousands of years. They include the First Nations, with diverse cultures from the fishing societies of the Pacific coast to the farming Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy in the east, the Inuit of the Arctic, and later the Métis, of mixed Indigenous and European ancestry.
Norse explorers reached Newfoundland around 1000 CE, establishing a short-lived settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows.

history.heading: New France and British North America
paragraphs: John Cabot reached the Atlantic coast in 1497, and Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River in the 1530s. Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608, the heart of New France. The fur trade drove exploration and relations with Indigenous peoples.

Britain conquered New France in the Seven Years' War, with the decisive battle at Quebec in 1759. The Quebec Act of 1774 protected French language, civil law and the Catholic religion. After the American Revolution, thousands of Loyalists moved north. The British colonies repelled American invasions in the War of 1812.

history.heading: Confederation and growth
paragraphs: On 1 July 1867, Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick united to form the Dominion of Canada. The country expanded westward, completed a transcontinental railway in 1885 and attracted millions of immigrants.

Expansion came at great cost to Indigenous peoples, through treaties, loss of land and the residential school system, which forcibly removed Indigenous children from their families for over a century; the government apologised in 2008, and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015.

history.heading: An independent nation
paragraphs: Canada's contributions in the world wars, including the Battle of Vimy Ridge in 1917, strengthened national identity. The 1931 Statute of Westminster gave it legislative independence, and in 1982 the constitution was patriated with a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Quebec's Quiet Revolution in the 1960s transformed the province, and independence referendums in 1980 and 1995 were narrowly defeated. In 1999 the territory of Nunavut was created with an Inuit majority. In 2025, Canada's relations with the United States were strained by US tariffs and talk of annexation.

culture.heading: A bilingual, multicultural country
paragraphs: English and French are the official languages; French is the majority language in Quebec, and there are French-speaking communities elsewhere, such as the Acadians. Canada officially adopted multiculturalism in 1971 and has one of the highest immigration rates in the world, with large communities from India, China, the Philippines and elsewhere.
Indigenous cultures, languages and art are increasingly recognised as central to Canadian identity.

culture.heading: Arts and identity
paragraphs: Canada has produced writers such as Margaret Atwood and Alice Munro, a Nobel laureate, and musicians from Joni Mitchell and Leonard Cohen to Céline Dion, Drake and The Weeknd. The Group of Seven painters celebrated Canadian landscapes.
Canadian food includes poutine (fries with cheese curds and gravy), maple syrup, butter tarts and Nanaimo bars.

culture.heading: Sport
paragraphs: Ice hockey is the national winter sport and a passion; lacrosse is the national summer sport. Basketball was invented by a Canadian, James Naismith. Canadians also love curling, skiing and Canadian football.

politics.heading: Federal parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: Canada is a federal parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, with the British monarch as King of Canada, represented by a governor general. The prime minister leads the government, which must have the confidence of the elected House of Commons; the Senate is appointed.

The ten provinces have substantial powers, including over health and education, while three territories in the north have more limited autonomy. The main parties are the Liberals and Conservatives, with the New Democratic Party and the Bloc Québécois also represented.

politics.heading: Foreign relations
paragraphs: Canada is a founding member of NATO and a member of the G7, the Commonwealth and La Francophonie. The United States is its closest partner, linked by the world's longest undefended border and deep economic ties, though US tariffs from 2025 pushed Canada to diversify its trade and security partnerships.

economy.heading: Resources and services
paragraphs: Canada has one of the world's largest economies and high living standards. It is rich in natural resources, with major oil reserves, mainly in Alberta's oil sands, as well as natural gas, minerals, timber and fresh water. It is a large exporter of oil, cars, wheat, canola and potash.
Services dominate the economy, including finance, real estate, technology and tourism. Toronto is a major financial centre. The currency is the Canadian dollar.

economy.heading: Trade and challenges
paragraphs: Around three-quarters of exports go to the United States, under the USMCA free trade agreement with the US and Mexico, which makes Canada vulnerable to US trade policy. Key challenges include housing affordability, low productivity growth, and balancing resource development with climate commitments and Indigenous rights.
